chunks: Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Masrur (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amir narrated to us, from his uncle 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Malik ibn 'Atiyya, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, from the Master of Worshippers 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), who said:

The believer blends his knowledge with forbearance. He sits to learn, listens to be safe, and speaks to make understood. He does not disclose what he has been trusted with even to his friends, nor does he withhold his testimony from his enemies. He does not perform any righteous deed out of ostentation, nor does he leave it out of shyness. If he is praised, he fears what they say, and he seeks God's forgiveness for what they do not know. He is not deceived by the praise of those who do not know him, and he is mindful of the reckoning of those who do know him.

The hypocrite forbids but does not restrain himself, and commands what he himself does not do. When he stands in prayer, he complains; when he bows, he slumps; when he prostrates, he pecks; and when he sits, he sprawls. He spends his evening preoccupied with food, even though he is not fasting; and he wakes up in the morning preoccupied with sleep, even though he did not stay up the night. If he speaks to you, he lies; if he makes a promise to you, he breaks it; if you entrust him with something, he betrays it; and if you disagree with him, he backbites you.

key_terms.إِحْصَاء: Divine reckoning and enumeration — the believer remains conscious that God counts every deed, even if people are ignorant
key_terms.الحِلْم: Forbearance, clemency — the capacity to absorb provocation without reacting rashly; a Quranic virtue often paired with knowledge
key_terms.الْمُنَافِق: The hypocrite — one who displays outward faith while harboring inward disbelief or corruption; a serious category in Islamic theology
key_terms.حَيَاء: Modesty, shyness — while generally praiseworthy, the Imam warns against letting it cause one to omit obligatory acts
key_terms.رِيَاء: Ostentation, showing off religious acts for people's admiration — a form of hidden shirk in Islamic ethics

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sajjad say about the differences between a true believer and a hypocrite?
ai.summary: Imam 'Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Sajjad (peace be upon him), the fourth Imam of the Shia Muslims, drew a vivid contrast between the true believer and the hypocrite across multiple domains of character and conduct. The believer is defined by the integration of knowledge with wisdom and humility: he learns, listens, and speaks purposefully, acts righteously without seeking praise, and remains vigilant of divine accountability even when humans praise him. In contrast, the hypocrite is defined by the complete disjunction between his outward commands and his own behavior: he preaches what he does not practice, performs worship carelessly, and in personal dealings is a liar, promise-breaker, traitor, and backbiter. This teaching was particularly significant in the context of the early Islamic community after Karbala (61 AH), when Imam al-Sajjad faced a community of nominal Muslims whose sincerity was questionable.
